prompt: Order the stages of the software development lifecycle for a new feature.

task.prompt: Drag the items into the right order, first at the top.

items.label: Design: UX screens and technical design
Requirements: agree what the feature must do

task.explanation: Requirements, design, build, test, deploy, maintain. Agile teams repeat this loop in small slices every sprint.

prompt: Order what happens to a single user story in a typical agency sprint.

task.prompt: Drag the items into the right order, first at the top.

items.label: Product owner accepts it at the sprint review
Merged and deployed to the QA/staging environment
Developer picks it up and creates a branch
Pull request opened and code reviewed
QA tests it against the acceptance criteria

task.explanation: Refine, build on a branch, review, merge and deploy to a test environment, test, then accept.

prompt: Mark the problems in this project plan for a client mobile app.

task.prompt: Mark every segment that is a problem. Leave the sound ones unmarked.

segments.text: Weeks 3-4: UX design and technical architecture.
Testing: none planned, developers will test their own code.
segments.issue: No independent QA; bugs reach the client and production.

segments.text: Week 15: launch to app stores on Monday, client announces it on Tuesday.
segments.issue: No buffer for app-store review, which can take days and may reject the build.

prompt: Fixing a defect gets more expensive the later it is found. Using the agency's rule-of-thumb costs, work out the cost of these bugs.

task.prompt: Calculate each value from the data.

fields.label: Total cost of fixing all bugs found
Saving if the 2 production bugs had been caught in QA instead

task.explanation: Design: 10 × $100 = $1,000; QA: 6 × $400 = $2,400; production: 2 × $1,500 = $3,000. Total $6,400. Catching the 2 production bugs in QA saves 2 × $1,100 = $2,200.

prompt: A client asks why the team needs a 'technical design' step before coding a new loyalty-points feature. They want developers to start today.

task.prompt: A client asks why the team needs a 'technical design' step before coding a new loyalty-points feature. They want developers to start today.

steps.question: How do you explain it?
options: A short design catches data-model and integration problems early, when they are cheap to change
steps.explanation: Explain value in the client's terms: lower cost and risk.

steps.question: The feature is tiny (one new label). What do you do?
options: Insist on a full design document
Scale the design to the risk: a quick note in the ticket is enough
steps.explanation: SDLC steps should be proportionate to the size and risk of the change.

prompt: A developer says a feature is 'done' because the code works on their laptop.

task.prompt: A developer says a feature is 'done' because the code works on their laptop.

steps.question: Is the feature done?
options: Not yet: it still needs review, testing and deployment per the Definition of Done
Yes, if the client has not complained
Only if it has comments in the code
steps.explanation: 'Works on my machine' is just the development step; done includes review, testing and deployment.

steps.question: What helps the team share one meaning of 'done'?
steps.explanation: A Definition of Done makes the quality bar explicit and shared.

prompt: What does QA mean in a software team?

options: Quality assurance: checking the software meets requirements and finding defects
mcq.explanation: QA verifies that what was built works as intended before it reaches users.

prompt: In which SDLC stage are wireframes and screen designs usually produced?

mcq.explanation: Wireframes and UI designs come out of the design stage, before development.

prompt: How does an agile team use the SDLC differently from a waterfall team?

options: It runs all the stages in small loops each sprint instead of once for the whole project
It only deploys once at the end
mcq.explanation: Agile still plans, designs, builds, tests and deploys, but in short iterations on small slices of work.
